review.title: Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow
review.summary: The paper introduces a mathematical framework for deterministic nonperiodic flow using finite systems of ordinary differential equations representing forced dissipative hydrodynamic systems. It proves that bounded nonperiodic central trajectories are unstable, implying that small errors in initial conditions grow over time, making long-range prediction impossible. A three-equation convection model is numerically integrated using a double-approximation scheme, yielding a nonperiodic solution. The author argues that all solutions of this model are unstable and almost all are nonperiodic, and discusses implications for weather forecasting, concluding that precise very-long-range forecasting is impossible due to inevitable observational errors.

strengths.point: A key theoretical result shows that any stable central trajectory must be quasi-periodic; therefore a nonperiodic central trajectory is necessarily unstable, linking nonperiodicity directly to practical unpredictability.
strengths.quote: It follows immediately that a stable central trajectory is quasi-periodic, or, equivalently, that a nonperiodic central trajectory is unstable.

strengths.point: The double-approximation numerical procedure is presented as an improvement over forward and centered differences, preserving the deterministic nature of the equations while providing a practical integration scheme.
strengths.quote: A procedure which largely overcomes the disadvantages of both the forward-difference and centered-difference procedures is the double-approximation procedure, defined by the relation X_{i,n+1} = X_{i,n} + 1/2[F_i(P_n) + F_i(P_{(n+1)})]Δt.

strengths.point: The paper explicitly connects the mathematical instability result to the real-world problem of weather prediction, acknowledging that observational errors make precise long-range forecasting impossible.
strengths.quote: If, then, there is any error whatever in observing the present state—and in any real system such errors seem inevitable—an acceptable prediction of an instantaneous state in the distant future may well be impossible.

strengths.point: The conclusion honestly discusses the limitations of applying the idealized model to the atmosphere, noting that the atmosphere may not be deterministic or finite and that 'very-long-range' is not quantified.
strengths.quote: One does not usually regard the atmosphere as either deterministic or finite, and the lack of periodicity is not a mathematical certainty, since the atmosphere has not been observed forever.

concerns.point: The claim that 'all solutions are unstable, and almost all of them are nonperiodic' is based on a single numerical integration from one initial condition (0,1,0) and one parameter set (σ=10, r=28, b=8/3). The periodic solutions are asserted to exist analytically but their instability is not numerically demonstrated.
concerns.quote: For initial conditions we have chosen a slight departure from the state of no convection, namely (0,1,0). ... All solutions, and in particular the periodic solutions, are found to be unstable. The remaining solutions therefore cannot in general approach the periodic solutions asymptotically, and so are nonperiodic.
concerns.suggestion: The authors should either provide numerical evidence for multiple initial conditions and parameter values, or clearly state that the generality of the claim is a conjecture supported only by the single computed trajectory and the theoretical argument for periodic solutions.

concerns.point: The paper dismisses the possibility of stable noncentral nonperiodic trajectories as 'not characteristic of real hydrodynamical phenomena' without proof, yet the claim that all nonperiodic trajectories are effectively unstable rests on this dismissal.
concerns.quote: The possibility of a nonperiodic noncentral trajectory which is stable but not uniformly stable still exists. To the writer, at least, such trajectories, although possible on paper, do not seem characteristic of real hydrodynamical phenomena.
concerns.suggestion: Either provide a dynamical-systems argument why such trajectories are unlikely in forced dissipative systems, or weaken the conclusion to apply only to central trajectories and to noncentral trajectories that are uniformly stable.

concerns.point: The printed tables multiply values by 10 and truncate to integers, losing precision and making it difficult to verify the numerical solution from the published data.
concerns.quote: In the printed output (but not in the computations) the values of X, Y, and Z are multiplied by ten, and then only those figures to the left of the decimal point are printed.
concerns.suggestion: Note that the full-precision values are available upon request, or provide a sample of the untruncated output.

withdrawn.point: The double-approximation procedure uses ambiguous notation: P_{(n+1)} in equation (13) could refer to the forward-difference estimate (9) or the centered-difference estimate (10), and the derivation of equation (14) from (9) and (10) is not clearly explained.
withdrawn.why: The concern misidentifies equation (10) as the centered-difference estimate; the paper defines P_{(n+1)} using the forward-difference estimate (9) and the centered-difference procedure is given separately in equation (12).

withdrawn.point: The time step Δt used in the numerical integration is never specified, making it impossible to assess the accuracy of the integration or to reproduce the results.
withdrawn.why: The paper specifies the dimensionless time step Δτ=0.01, contrary to the referee's claim that it is never specified.

checklist.quote: A trajectory P(t) will be called stable at a point P(t_1) if any other trajectory passing sufficiently close to P(t_1) at time t_1 remains close to P(t) as t→∞
checklist.note: Stability is defined qualitatively; no quantitative metric (e.g., Lyapunov exponent) is introduced.

checklist.quote: One does not usually regard the atmosphere as either deterministic or finite, and the lack of periodicity is not a mathematical certainty, since the atmosphere has not been observed forever.
checklist.note: The conclusion explicitly addresses the idealizations and their relevance to the real atmosphere.

questions: What is the time step Δt used in the numerical integration, and how was it chosen?
Were any other initial conditions or parameter values explored to support the claim that 'all solutions are unstable'?
Can the double-approximation procedure be clarified: does P_{(n+1)} in equation (13) refer to the forward-difference estimate (9) or the centered-difference estimate (10)?
The paper dismisses noncentral stable nonperiodic trajectories as not characteristic of real hydrodynamical phenomena. What is the basis for this physical intuition?
How does the truncation of output values (multiplying by 10 and taking integer part) affect the interpretation of the numerical results, especially for small values?

related.assessment: The paper's core contribution—proving instability of bounded nonperiodic trajectories in a deterministic hydrodynamic ODE system and linking it to weather predictability limits—appears distinct from these results, which focus on numerical methods for convection rather than dynamical systems theory. The 1986 Knobloch et al. work is the closest conceptually but addresses double-diffusive convection specifically, not the general framework or prediction impossibility argument. The novelty of the 'deterministic nonperiodic flow' framework and its philosophical implication for forecasting cannot be fully judged without comparing the full mathematical proofs and the specific three-equation model against the cited convection literature.

figures.4: Figure 4 is a scatter plot with a single data series. The x-axis is labeled "M_n" (abscissa) and ranges from 0 to 0.5. The y-axis is labeled "M_n+1" (ordinate) and ranges from 300 to 450. The plot shows a sharp, triangular peak centered around M_n ≈ 0.25, with M_n+1 reaching a maximum of approximately 450 at this point. The data points form a dense cluster forming the peak, with values decreasing symmetrically on either side as M_n moves away from 0.25. The caption states that these are "Corresponding values of relative maximum of Z (abscissa) and subsequent relative maximum of Z (ordinate) occurring during the first 6000 iterations."
figures.5: Figure 5 is a line graph with the title "The function $M_{n+1} = 2M_n$ if $M_n < \frac{1}{2}$, $M_{n+1} = 2 - 2M_n$ if $M_n > \frac{1}{2}$, serving as an idealization of the locus of points in Fig. 4." The graph has two axes: the horizontal axis (abscissa) is labeled "0" at the left and "1" at the right, with a tick mark at "0.5" in the middle. The vertical axis (ordinate) is labeled "0" at the bottom and "1" at the top, with tick marks at "0" and "1". The graph shows a single triangular shape: it starts at the point (0, 0), rises sharply to a peak at (0.5, 1), and then falls sharply back to (1, 0). The line forming the triangle is straight and continuous. There are no additional labels, data points, or annotations visible on the graph itself, only the axes and the triangular shape.
